extracted.intended_audience: householders (especially women), family caregivers, and home nurses
extracted.subtask_description: Practical domestic guidance on personal hygiene, digestive care, nursing the sick, temperance, cheerfulness, and family musical education for householders and caregivers. Includes specific do's and don'ts, examples, and some first-aid directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care of the stomach / digestive hygiene
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize prevention over remedial dosing; soothe rather than punish an irritated stomach; fasting and careful diet are preferred to heavy medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If upset, fast for a few hours until faintness warns to eat; then eat slowly small, light foods (milk-toast, hot beef-tea). Quiet and diet are more effective than quarts of medicine. Avoid 'taking a course of physic' as a matter of principle when not needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid known dietary irritants
rubrics_metrics.description: Be reasonably careful about foods that disagree with you; if a particular food has caused dyspepsia, abstain from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dyspeptics should eschew hot breads, pastry, fried or greasy food, nuts and many sweets. Avoid dependence on remedies (e.g., bicarbonate of soda) to mask poor diet; large and frequent doses of some 'correctives' may be harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin cleanliness and keeping pores open
rubrics_metrics.description: The skin disposes of impurities; pores must be kept open by frequent washing to prevent illness from retained effete matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use soap and warm water regularly; sponge the entire body daily, especially in creases where perspiration accumulates. Plunge baths are recommended to open pores and thoroughly cleanse the surface. Do not neglect covered parts of the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular, appropriate exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise should be regular and abundant but not excessive; everyday activities often suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Housework and walking are generally sufficient for women; horseback riding, rowing and tennis are beneficial for pleasure and health but avoid over-weariness. Balance activity with rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient sleep and restorative naps
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure enough night sleep to prevent daytime drowsiness; elderly or feeble persons may benefit from a noonday nap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid chronic sleep deprivation; do not accept being 'constitutionally tired' as normal. Short naps after the midday meal during warm weather refresh older or frail people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheerfulness as a duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate cheerfulness for the benefit of oneself and others; avoid indulgence in imaginary or sentimental sorrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine grief (sympathy required) from self-indulgent sentimentality. Practice cheerful courage: work and play wholeheartedly; use good humor to lighten burdens and improve character. Avoid preparing for 'smileless eternity' by banishing gaiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against habitual melancholy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some inherit a tendency toward morbidness and must exercise vigilance to prevent habitual gloom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habitual sadness grows like fungus; counter it by cultivating habitually cheerful responses, laughing over vexations to dissipate their sting, and engaging in life-affirming activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain quiet and an orderly atmosphere in the sick-room
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve 'Dr. Quiet' in the chamber of illness: eliminate noise, avoid whispering and prevent excitement that may harm the patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wear soft slippers; speak in a low-pitched undertone rather than whispering (whispering arouses curiosity); forbid loud tones, exclamations, political or religious controversy in hearing of the patient. Do not let the patient worry about household duties or inconveniences caused by illness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness in the sick-room and patient care
rubrics_metrics.description: Immaculate cleanliness in every detail is essential: sponge the patient, clean teeth and hair, change gowns and bed-linen frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponge the sick person all over daily when disease permits; wash face and hands often; change sheets frequently. If safe, roll or move the patient to change and remake bed; beat pillows and air bedding. Keep the room aired without chilling the patient; avoid overheating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper clothing for comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Dress the sick in comfortable, practical garments that allow warmth and freedom of movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a flannel 'nightingale' or jacket over the shoulders to leave arms free; cover patient warmly when airing room briefly. Avoid constricting or inappropriate clothing that causes discomfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food presentation and portioning for the sick
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare the patient's tray daintily in small portions to avoid discouraging a weak appetite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choicest china and whitest linen; give very little at a time (a small bird, one chop, or a bit of tender meat). Avoid loaded plates; present one item at a time if necessary (e.g., one oyster at a time) to stimulate appetite and make food seem specially allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow physician's directions when administering medicine
rubrics_metrics.description: Strict adherence to the doctor's prescribed quantity and timing is required; avoid alarming the patient by ritualizing dosing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prepare the dose in the patient's presence; after the medicine is swallowed, put bottle and spoon out of sight. Measure precisely and observe timing as ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early home treatment before the doctor arrives
rubrics_metrics.description: Some immediate measures may be taken sensibly before professional help arrives, but with caution due to potent remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a child with fever/hoarseness: soak the feet in hot water, put to bed, and consider an anti-febrile (aconite) until slight perspiration is induced. (The text gives an aconite dose: half a drop in a teaspoonful of water every hour for ages three to six—note: historical advice and potentially dangerous by modern standards.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mothers should learn children's ailments and diets
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents, especially mothers, ought to study common childhood illnesses and appropriate dietary care so they are neither ignorant nor negligent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train children to take medicine and to accept prescribed diets without resistance. Understand what foods are digestible during illness and avoid offering conglomerations of indigestible substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nurse and patient should both practice self-control and cheerfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual gentleness, gratitude, and self-control between patient and nurse improve recovery and the atmosphere of the sick-room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nurses should avoid fussiness, maintain calm efficiency, and not display worry. Patients should be gentle and appreciative rather than unduly querulous; both should practice forbearance to bring light into suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid causing the patient needless anxiety about household affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent the invalid from imagining burdens their illness imposes; do not let them worry about inconveniences or unfinished work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never allow remarks or demeanor that suggest the patient's illness is an annoyance or unduly inconvenient. Act decently, rapidly, and quietly in household tasks to reassure the patient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance: abstain from beverages that 'make drunk come'
rubrics_metrics.description: Total abstinence from drinks likely to produce intoxication is urged; social or 'mannish' drinking as proof of steadiness is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author detests drinking that leads to drunkenness; regards even occasional social dram-drinking as risky because a glass may become three and then an addiction. Condemns vanity-driven drinking and the social pressures that encourage it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance: discourage enabling and social approval of drinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals and communities should not tacitly approve or encourage social drinking, nor give liquor to those predisposed to inebriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should not lend example or assist in providing intoxicants; 'Woe unto him that putteth the cup to his neighbor's lips.' Social conviviality that tempts weak brothers is morally culpable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance: accept limited medicinal and culinary uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Alcohol may be retained for strictly medicinal purposes and sparing culinary uses, provided no one in the household is tempted or addicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure brandy, wine and whiskey have value as restoratives by physician prescription. Small culinary quantities (tablespoonful in pudding or a wineglass in jelly) pose no danger unless taken by someone already craving stimulants; omit them if a guest or family member is predisposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family musical education
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage vocal and instrumental music at home: singing by note, use of song collections, and keyboard instruction for girls as part of household culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, families used collections like the Boston Academy and Carmina Sacra; nearly every household sang by note and girls were taught pianoforte. Maintain communal music-making rather than costly virtuoso performance as a means of family enrichment.
